name: Wurtz Reaction
summary: Alkyl halides couple with sodium metal in dry ether to form a symmetrical alkane with double the number of carbons.
mechanism: Na transfers an electron to R–X giving an alkyl radical/organosodium (R–Na) species. The carbanion-like R–Na attacks a second R–X in an SN2 step, expelling X- and forming the C–C bond.
keyPoints: Gives only symmetrical alkanes (R–R) cleanly; a mixture of two different RX gives three alkanes (R–R, R–R'', R''–R'') that are hard to separate
Methane cannot be prepared (needs at least 2 C in product)
Tertiary halides undergo elimination to alkene instead
Dry ether is essential because Na reacts with water
Product has twice the carbon count of the alkyl halide
whenUsed: Laboratory preparation of symmetrical higher alkanes with an even number of carbon atoms.

examples.eq: CH3Cl + C2H5Cl + 2 Na ->[\text{dry ether}] CH3CH2CH3 + 2 NaCl
examples.note: Unsymmetrical coupling gives mixture (also ethane + butane)

jeeTips: To make an odd-carbon alkane such as propane you cannot use Wurtz cleanly. Product carbon count = 2 x carbon of RX. Using Li or Zn instead is Frankland-type; do not confuse with Wurtz–Fittig (aryl halide + alkyl halide).

name: Corey–House Synthesis
summary: An alkyl halide is converted to lithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent), which couples with a second alkyl halide to give an unsymmetrical alkane in good yield.
mechanism: R-X + 2 Li gives R-Li; 2 R-Li + CuI gives R2CuLi. The cuprate then undergoes SN2-type coupling with R''-X forming R-R'' and R-Cu.
keyPoints: Preferred over Wurtz for preparing unsymmetrical alkanes (odd or even carbon count)
R''X should preferably be primary (methyl/1° halide); R in the cuprate can be 1°, 2° or 3°
Overall: R–X to R2CuLi to R–R''
Also couples with aryl and vinyl halides
whenUsed: Clean synthesis of unsymmetrical alkanes where Wurtz would give a mixture.
jeeTips: Asked as a better alternative to Wurtz: the answer is Corey–House (R2CuLi + R''X). Remember it is R2CuLi, not R–MgX; Grignard reagents do not give this clean coupling with alkyl halides.

name: Kolbe's Electrolysis
summary: Electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid gives a symmetrical alkane at the anode, with CO2 and, at the cathode, H2 and NaOH.
mechanism: At the anode RCOO- loses an electron to give RCOO. which loses CO2 to form R.; two R. radicals dimerise to R–R. At the cathode water is reduced giving H2 and OH-.
keyPoints: Anode: 2 RCOO- -> R-R + 2 CO2 + 2 e-
Cathode: 2 H2O + 2 e- -> H2 + 2 OH-
Sodium acetate gives ethane; sodium succinate gives ethene; sodium maleate/fumarate gives ethyne
Mixture of two salts gives three alkanes
Number of C in alkane = 2 x (C in R)
whenUsed: Synthesis of even-carbon symmetrical alkanes, alkenes (from dicarboxylates) and alkynes.
jeeTips: Products at the anode: alkane + CO2; at the cathode: H2 (not the alkane). For HCOONa you get H2 and CO2 only. Dicarboxylate with n carbons between gives alkene/alkyne - count carbons carefully.

name: Decarboxylation with Soda Lime
summary: Heating sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime removes the carboxylate as carbonate, giving an alkane with one carbon fewer.
mechanism: Hydroxide attacks the carboxylate carbon region; heterolytic loss of CO3 2- generates a carbanion R- that is protonated by water/NaOH to give R–H.
keyPoints: Descent of the series: lowers carbon count by one (step-down)
Soda lime = NaOH + CaO (3:1); CaO keeps NaOH from absorbing moisture and prevents fusing/attacking glass
Free acid itself does not decarboxylate this way
Sodium acetate gives methane
Dicarboxylate salts give alkane after losing both CO2 groups as carbonate
whenUsed: Laboratory preparation of methane and for converting a carboxylic acid into the alkane with one carbon fewer.
jeeTips: Compare: Kolbe gives R–R (even carbon, aqueous electrolysis); soda lime gives R–H (carbon minus 1). Reaction needs the sodium salt, not the acid.

name: Sabatier–Senderens Reduction
aliases: Catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes
catalyst: Finely divided Ni (Sabatier–Senderens); Pt, Pd at room temp
summary: Alkenes and alkynes add hydrogen over finely divided Ni (at 200–300 °C) or Pt/Pd (room temp) to give the saturated alkane.
mechanism: H2 is adsorbed on the metal surface and dissociates into atoms; the alkene is also adsorbed and both H atoms are delivered to the same face, giving syn addition.
keyPoints: Syn addition of H2 from the metal surface
Ni needs 200–300 °C (Sabatier–Senderens); Pt/Pd work at ordinary temperature
Alkyne goes through alkene to alkane with excess H2
Exothermic: heat of hydrogenation measures alkene stability
Also reduces C=O, NO2, CN groups under suitable conditions
whenUsed: Industrial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (to vanaspati), and laboratory preparation of alkanes.

examples.note: Ethyne to ethane with excess H2

jeeTips: Heat of hydrogenation: more substituted/trans alkene is more stable so has lower value. Excess H2/Ni takes alkyne all the way to alkane, only Lindlar or Na/NH3 stop at alkene.

name: Reduction of Alkyl Halides with Zn/HCl
summary: Alkyl halides are reduced to alkanes with the same carbon skeleton by nascent hydrogen from Zn and dilute HCl.
mechanism: Zn donates electrons to the C–X bond (single electron transfer) producing carbanion/radical equivalents which are protonated by H+ from the acid.
keyPoints: Carbon skeleton is unchanged; X is replaced by H
Other reducing agents: LiAlH4, Zn–Cu/C2H5OH, red P + HI, H2/Pd
Zn/HCl on carbonyl compounds is Clemmensen reduction, not this reaction
Ease of reduction: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F
whenUsed: Preparation of alkane from alkyl halide with no change in carbon count.
jeeTips: Remember trio: Wurtz (R–R, carbon doubled), Kolbe (R–R), Zn/HCl (R–H, same carbons), soda lime (R–H, one carbon less).

name: Free-Radical Halogenation of Alkanes
summary: Alkanes react with Cl2 or Br2 in UV light or at high temperature in a radical chain substitution, replacing H by halogen.
mechanism: Initiation: X2 splits into 2 X. by light. Propagation: X. + R–H gives R. + HX; R. + X2 gives R–X + X.. Termination: radical pairs combine (X–X, R–X, R–R).
keyPoints: Reactivity of H: 3° > 2° > 1° (stability of radicals)
Reactivity of halogen: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 (I2 is reversible and does not react)
Bromination is much more selective than chlorination
Polysubstitution happens unless alkane is in large excess
Radical intermediate is planar so chiral centre racemises
whenUsed: Industrial production of CH2Cl2, CHCl3, CCl4; mechanism-based selectivity questions.
jeeTips: Count monochloro isomers (including stereoisomers) by multiplying number of distinct H types with reactivity weights. Br2 gives mainly 3° product; Cl2 gives a mixture. I2 reaction is endothermic so does not occur.

name: Dehydrohalogenation (Saytzeff Rule)
summary: Heating an alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH removes HX in a β-elimination to give the more substituted (more stable) alkene as the major product.
mechanism: E2: base removes the β-H while X- leaves simultaneously from the anti-periplanar position, forming the C=C. The transition state resembles the alkene, so the more substituted alkene is favoured.
keyPoints: Saytzeff rule: more highly substituted alkene is major
Aqueous KOH gives substitution (alcohol); alcoholic KOH gives elimination
Order of ease: 3° > 2° > 1° halide; R–I > R–Br > R–Cl
Anti-periplanar geometry decides cis/trans or stereospecific alkene in rigid rings
Trans-alkene is usually major over cis
whenUsed: Common route to alkenes from haloalkanes; vicinal dihalide with alc. KOH/NaNH2 gives alkynes.
jeeTips: KOH(aq) = SN; KOH(alc) = E. The main trap: bulky base (t-BuOK) reverses to Hofmann product. Also check for rearrangement-free E2 vs E1 in tertiary substrates.

name: Hofmann Elimination Preference with Bulky Base (t-BuOK)
summary: With a sterically hindered base such as potassium tert-butoxide the less hindered β-hydrogen is removed, giving the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product) as the major product.
mechanism: The bulky base cannot easily approach the internal, more crowded β-hydrogen, so abstracts the more accessible terminal β-H in an E2 step to give the terminal alkene.
keyPoints: Hofmann rule: less substituted alkene is major
Also seen in elimination of quaternary ammonium hydroxides (Hofmann elimination) and with large leaving groups (F-, NR3+, SR2+)
Base size controls selectivity, not just substrate
Small bases (OEt-, OH-) give Saytzeff
whenUsed: Used to obtain terminal alkenes selectively from secondary/tertiary halides.
jeeTips: Questions compare alc. KOH (Saytzeff) vs t-BuOK (Hofmann). Also remember Hofmann elimination of R4N+ OH- gives least substituted alkene.

name: Dehydration of Alcohols (Conc. H2SO4)
summary: Alcohols lose water on heating with conc. H2SO4 (or H3PO4, alumina at 623 K) to give alkenes, following Saytzeff orientation.
mechanism: The OH is protonated to –OH2+; water leaves giving a carbocation (E1) which loses a β-H to form the alkene. Carbocation may rearrange (hydride/methyl shift) before elimination.
keyPoints: Ease of dehydration: 3° > 2° > 1°
Temperature matters: ethanol at 443 K gives ethene; at 413 K gives diethyl ether (intermolecular)
Major alkene is the more substituted (Saytzeff)
Carbocation rearrangement possible for 1° and 2° alcohols
Needs β-hydrogen
whenUsed: Laboratory ethene; industrial route to alkenes; route in multi-step synthesis.
jeeTips: Temperature switch: 443 K alkene vs 413 K ether (excess alcohol). Neopentyl-type alcohols rearrange. Cyclic examples frequently involve ring expansion.

name: Markovnikov Addition of HX
aliases: Electrophilic addition of HX to alkenes
summary: Hydrogen halides add across an unsymmetrical alkene so that H goes to the carbon with more hydrogens and X to the more substituted carbon.
mechanism: The π bond attacks H+ to give the more stable carbocation (3° > 2° > 1°); halide ion then attacks the carbocation. Because a free carbocation forms, rearrangement can occur.
keyPoints: Markovnikov: negative part goes to the carbon with fewer H
Order of reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl
Rearrangement of carbocation possible (e.g. 3-methylbut-1-ene to 2-bromo-2-methylbutane)
Product with chiral centre is racemic (planar carbocation)
Ethene + HX gives only one product
whenUsed: Synthesis of secondary and tertiary haloalkanes from alkenes.
jeeTips: Look for rearrangement in carbocation questions. Anti-Markovnikov occurs only with HBr + peroxide, not with HCl or HI. For CF3CH=CH2 and similar –I groups, addition is anti-Markovnikov.

name: Peroxide Effect (Kharasch Anti-Markovnikov Addition of HBr)
summary: In the presence of peroxides, HBr adds to unsymmetrical alkenes against Markovnikov orientation through a free-radical chain.
mechanism: Peroxide gives RO. which abstracts H from HBr to give Br.. Br. adds to the alkene at the less substituted carbon to form the more stable carbon radical, which abstracts H from another HBr, regenerating Br..
keyPoints: Works only with HBr (HCl: H–Cl bond too strong; HI: I. adds reversibly/H–I step endothermic overall)
Br adds to the terminal (less substituted) carbon
Free-radical chain mechanism with more stable radical
Symmetrical alkenes show no difference
Alkynes also show peroxide effect with HBr
whenUsed: Prepares primary alkyl bromides from terminal alkenes.

examples.note: No peroxide effect for HCl: still Markovnikov

jeeTips: Peroxide effect: only HBr. If question gives HCl or HI with peroxide, product is Markovnikov. Peroxide-free conditions also described as "dark" in older papers.

name: Hydroboration–Oxidation
summary: Diborane adds to alkenes syn and anti-Markovnikov to give trialkylboranes, which on oxidation with alkaline H2O2 give the alcohol with net anti-Markovnikov hydration.
mechanism: BH3 adds in a concerted four-centre step: B to the less hindered carbon, H to the more substituted carbon, on the same face. Then H2O2/OH- replaces C–B with C–OH with retention.
keyPoints: Anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry
Syn addition; no carbocation so no rearrangement
Terminal alkenes give primary alcohols; terminal alkynes (via R2BH) give aldehydes
Stereochemistry retained in oxidation step
Net: syn addition of H and OH
whenUsed: Method to prepare primary alcohols from terminal alkenes without rearrangement.
jeeTips: Compare three hydration routes: H3O+ (Markovnikov, rearranges), Hg(OAc)2/NaBH4 (Markovnikov, no rearrangement), BH3/H2O2 (anti-Markovnikov, syn, no rearrangement).

name: Oxymercuration–Demercuration
summary: Alkenes add water in a Markovnikov sense without carbocation rearrangement by treatment with mercuric acetate in water followed by NaBH4 reduction.
mechanism: Hg(OAc)+ forms a cyclic mercurinium ion; water attacks the more substituted carbon (anti addition) to give a β-hydroxy organomercurial; NaBH4 then replaces Hg by H.
keyPoints: Markovnikov regiochemistry
No carbocation rearrangement (bridged mercurinium ion)
Anti addition of OH and Hg in step 1
NaBH4 replaces HgOAc by H (stereochemistry lost)
In alcohol solvent gives ethers (alkoxymercuration)
whenUsed: Clean Markovnikov hydration of alkenes that would rearrange under H2O/H+.
jeeTips: Key contrast: H2O/H+ gives rearranged alcohol; oxymercuration gives unrearranged Markovnikov alcohol; hydroboration gives anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

name: Ozonolysis
summary: Ozone cleaves the C=C bond to an ozonide; reductive work-up (Zn/H2O or Me2S) gives aldehydes/ketones, oxidative work-up (H2O2) converts aldehydes to carboxylic acids.
mechanism: O3 adds to C=C to form a molozonide, which rearranges to the ozonide. Zn/H2O destroys H2O2 formed so aldehydes survive; H2O2 oxidises aldehyde fragments to RCOOH.
keyPoints: Each =CH2 gives HCHO (or HCOOH/CO2 on oxidative work-up)
=CHR gives RCHO (reductive) or RCOOH (oxidative); =CR2 gives ketone in both
Locates position of double bond in structure determination
Alkynes give 1,2-diketones / acids
Zn prevents over-oxidation by H2O2
whenUsed: Structure elucidation of unknown alkenes and in synthesis of carbonyl compounds.
jeeTips: Reverse-engineer alkene from fragments: join C=O carbons. Cyclic alkenes give dicarbonyl/diacid. Terminal =CH2 gives HCHO under reductive, CO2 under strong oxidative.

name: Baeyer's Test (Syn-Dihydroxylation with Cold Dilute KMnO4)
summary: Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO4 converts alkenes to cis-1,2-diols; the purple colour disappears and brown MnO2 precipitates, a test for C=C or C≡C unsaturation.
mechanism: Alkene attacks MnO4- forming a cyclic manganate(V) ester via concerted syn addition; hydrolysis releases the cis-diol and MnO2.
keyPoints: Syn addition gives cis-diol (cyclohexene gives cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol)
Purple colour fades, brown MnO2 forms - positive test for unsaturation
Needs cold, dilute, neutral/alkaline medium; hot or acidic cleaves
Also given by alkynes (more slowly), aldehydes, phenols, etc. so not specific
Alkene + MnO4- stoichiometry: 3 C=C : 2 MnO4-
whenUsed: Qualitative test for unsaturation; synthesis of 1,2-diols.

examples.eq: 3 CH2=CH2 + 2 KMnO4 + 4 H2O -> 3 HOCH2CH2OH + 2 MnO2 + 2 KOH

jeeTips: Syn (cis) diol with KMnO4/OsO4; anti (trans) diol with peracid then H3O+. Test is positive for any readily oxidisable group, not only C=C.

name: Hot KMnO4 Oxidative Cleavage of Alkenes
summary: Hot, acidic or concentrated KMnO4 breaks the C=C bond completely: =CR2 becomes ketone, =CHR becomes carboxylic acid, =CH2 becomes CO2 + H2O.
mechanism: Initial diol/manganate ester formed as in Baeyer test is further oxidised: the glycol C–C bond is cleaved to carbonyls and aldehydes are oxidised to acids.
keyPoints: =CH2 → CO2, =CHR → RCOOH, =CR2 → R2C=O
Alkynes give two carboxylic acids (terminal alkyne: RCOOH + CO2)
Cyclic alkenes give dicarboxylic acids (cyclohexene gives adipic acid)
Purple KMnO4 decolourised
Compare with ozonolysis (reductive gives aldehydes)
whenUsed: Structure determination of alkenes/alkynes; preparation of acids.
jeeTips: Differentiate: cold dilute (diol) vs hot/acidic (cleavage). For hot KMnO4 with R–CH=CH2, CO2 evolves (limewater turns milky).

name: Epoxidation with Peracid (Prilezhaev Reaction)
summary: Alkenes react with peroxy acids in a single concerted step to give epoxides (oxiranes) with retention of alkene geometry.
mechanism: The terminal O of the peracid is transferred to C=C through a cyclic "butterfly" transition state; the acid hydrogen goes to the carbonyl oxygen, giving the epoxide and carboxylic acid.
keyPoints: Stereospecific syn addition of O: cis-alkene gives cis-epoxide; trans-alkene gives trans-epoxide
Hydrolysis of epoxide with H3O+ gives trans-1,2-diol (anti)
Ethene + O2 over Ag at 520 K gives ethylene oxide (industrial)
Electron-rich alkenes react faster
Common peracids: mCPBA, peracetic acid, perbenzoic acid
whenUsed: Epoxide synthesis, then ring-opening to diols, amino alcohols, etc.
jeeTips: Peracid then H3O+ gives anti (trans) diol, whereas OsO4 or cold KMnO4 gives syn (cis) diol - favourite comparison.

name: OsO4 Dihydroxylation
summary: OsO4 adds to alkenes to give a cyclic osmate ester that is cleaved by NaHSO3 (or H2O/NMO) to give cis-1,2-diols in high yield.
mechanism: Concerted [3+2] addition of OsO4 to C=C forms a cyclic osmate(VI) ester; reductive hydrolysis liberates the diol and Os(IV).
keyPoints: Syn addition of two OH groups (cis-diol)
Cleaner than cold KMnO4 with less over-oxidation
Toxic and costly so used catalytically with NMO or H2O2
Stereospecific: cis-2-butene gives meso-diol; trans-2-butene gives racemic (±) diol
Both OsO4 and KMnO4 are syn; peracid/H3O+ is anti
whenUsed: Reliable synthesis of cis-diols and stereochemistry problems.
jeeTips: Stereochem trick: syn addition to cis alkene gives meso, to trans alkene gives racemic (for symmetrical 2-butene). Anti addition (peracid/H3O+) gives the opposite.

name: Lindlar's Catalyst Reduction
aliases: Partial hydrogenation of alkynes to cis-alkenes
catalyst: Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb(OAc)2 and quinoline
summary: Alkynes are hydrogenated only to the alkene stage over poisoned palladium (Lindlar) with syn addition, giving cis (Z)-alkenes.
mechanism: Both H atoms are delivered from the catalyst surface to the same face of the adsorbed alkyne (syn addition). Poisoning reduces Pd activity so the alkene desorbs before further reduction.
keyPoints: Syn addition gives cis (Z)-alkene
Pd/BaSO4 + quinoline (Rosenmund-type poisoning) is equivalent also called P-2 Ni (Ni2B) catalyst
Prevents over-reduction to alkane
Contrast: Na/liq NH3 gives trans (E)-alkene
Terminal alkyne gives terminal alkene
whenUsed: Stereoselective synthesis of cis-alkenes, e.g. pheromones and vitamin intermediates.
jeeTips: Lindlar = cis; Na/NH3 = trans. H2/Pd-C (unpoisoned) or Ni goes to alkane. Alkenes are not reduced by Na/NH3 at all.

name: Birch Reduction of Alkynes (Na/liq. NH3)
summary: Sodium (or Li) in liquid ammonia reduces internal alkynes to trans (E)-alkenes through radical anion/vinyl radical intermediates with overall anti addition of H2.
mechanism: Na gives an electron forming a radical anion; it is protonated by NH3 to a vinyl radical, which accepts another electron to form a trans-vinyl anion (more stable); second protonation gives the trans alkene.
keyPoints: Gives trans (E)-alkene with internal alkynes
Terminal alkynes are deprotonated by NaNH2 (formed) so do not reduce well
Alkenes themselves are not reduced under these conditions
Complementary to Lindlar (cis)
Ethanol or NH4Cl can be added as proton source
whenUsed: Stereoselective synthesis of trans-alkenes.
jeeTips: Na/NH3 (alkyne) = trans-alkene; Birch on benzene (Na/NH3, ROH) gives 1,4-cyclohexadiene. Same reagent, different substrates - do not confuse.

name: Acidic Hydration of Alkynes (Kucherov Reaction)
productName: Acetaldehyde (from ethyne); methyl ketones from other alkynes
summary: Alkynes add water in the presence of Hg2+ and dil. H2SO4 to give an enol that tautomerises to the carbonyl compound by Markovnikov addition.
mechanism: Hg2+ activates the triple bond; water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) to give a vinyl alcohol (enol), which undergoes keto–enol tautomerism to aldehyde or ketone.
keyPoints: Ethyne gives acetaldehyde (only alkyne giving an aldehyde)
All terminal alkynes (RC≡CH) give methyl ketones RCOCH3
Internal unsymmetrical alkynes give mixture of ketones
Enol intermediate is unstable (keto–enol tautomerism)
Contrast: hydroboration–oxidation of terminal alkyne gives aldehyde
whenUsed: Industrial route to acetaldehyde (older) and laboratory synthesis of ketones.
jeeTips: Only ethyne gives an aldehyde via Kucherov; hydroboration–oxidation of terminal alkyne also gives aldehyde (anti-Markovnikov). Know both.

name: Cyclic Polymerisation of Ethyne
summary: Three molecules of ethyne trimerise when passed through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K to give benzene.
mechanism: Pericyclic/metal-surface assisted cyclotrimerisation: three C≡C units link through successive coupling and aromatisation (each triple bond converts to a double bond in the ring).
keyPoints: 3 C2H2 gives C6H6 (carbon count conserved)
Propyne similarly gives mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene)
Ni(CO)2(PPh3)2 catalyst gives cyclooctatetraene from 4 C2H2 at 60–70 °C under pressure (Reppe)
Historical first synthesis of benzene from inorganic precursors
whenUsed: Synthesis of benzene from ethyne; synthetic link between aliphatic and aromatic series.
jeeTips: Ethyne to benzene: red-hot iron tube, 873 K. Not to be confused with CH≡CH + H2O (Kucherov) or acetylene + CuCl (vinylacetylene).

name: Acidity of Terminal Alkynes (NaNH2 and Tollens'' Test)
aliases: Ammoniacal AgNO3 test for terminal alkynes
productName: Sodium acetylide / silver or copper acetylide precipitate
summary: The sp C–H of terminal alkynes (pKa about 25) is acidic enough to be removed by NaNH2, and to give white silver acetylide or red copper acetylide precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO3 or Cu2Cl2.
mechanism: The sp-hybridised carbon (50% s-character) stabilises the lone pair in the conjugate base, so the proton is removed by strong bases (NH2-) or replaced by Ag+/Cu+.
keyPoints: Acidity order: HC≡CH > CH2=CH2 > CH3–CH3 (sp > sp2 > sp3)
Acetylide + RX gives higher alkynes (SN2 with 1° RX)
HC≡CH + 2 Ag(NH3)2+ gives white ppt of Ag2C2
R–C≡CH + Cu(NH3)2+ gives red ppt of R–C≡C–Cu
Internal alkynes (R–C≡C–R) do not react; metal acetylides explode when dry
Not acidic enough for NaOH or water to deprotonate
whenUsed: Distinguishing 1-alkynes from 2-alkynes and alkenes; chain extension via acetylides.

examples.eq: HC#CH + NaNH2 ->[\text{liq. NH3}] HC#C- Na+ + NH3

jeeTips: Ethene/ethane do not react with Tollens. 1-Butyne gives ppt; 2-butyne does not. Remember pKa order and sp s-character (50%).

name: Diels–Alder Reaction
summary: A conjugated diene reacts with a dienophile (alkene/alkyne, usually electron poor) in a concerted [4+2] cycloaddition to form a six-membered ring.
mechanism: The 4π electrons of the s-cis diene and 2π electrons of the dienophile reorganise in a single cyclic transition state forming two new σ bonds and one new π bond; thermal, suprafacial and stereospecific.
keyPoints: Diene must adopt s-cis conformation (cyclopentadiene is very reactive; locked s-trans dienes do not react)
Dienophile substituents (C=O, CN, NO2) speed the reaction
Stereospecific syn: cis substituents on dienophile remain cis in product
Endo rule: endo product is favoured kinetically (cyclic dienes)
Product with cyclic diene is bicyclic
whenUsed: Synthesis of six-membered rings, bicyclic compounds and in natural product synthesis.
jeeTips: Check s-cis requirement and electron demand. Product ring is 6-membered: total carbons = 4 (diene) + 2 (dienophile). Maleic anhydride is the standard dienophile; used as a test for conjugated dienes.

name: Allylic Bromination with NBS (Wohl–Ziegler)
summary: N-Bromosuccinimide substitutes allylic (and benzylic) hydrogens by bromine under radical conditions without attacking the C=C.
mechanism: NBS provides a very low steady concentration of Br2 (from HBr + NBS). Br. abstracts allylic H to give a resonance-stabilised allyl radical which reacts with Br2 to give allyl bromide and regenerates Br..
keyPoints: Low Br2 concentration prevents addition to C=C
Allylic and benzylic radical resonance stabilisation drives selectivity
Resonance can give rearranged product mixtures (allylic shift)
Benzylic bromination of toluene works the same way
Cyclohexene gives 3-bromocyclohexene
whenUsed: Selective introduction of Br at allylic/benzylic positions for further substitution/elimination (e.g. dienes).
jeeTips: Br2/CCl4 (dark) adds to C=C but NBS (low Br2) substitutes at allylic position. Resonance can place Br at the other end of the allyl system - watch for unsymmetrical alkenes.

name: Friedel–Crafts Alkylation
catalyst: AlCl3 (Lewis acid); FeCl3, BF3, HF also
summary: Benzene reacts with alkyl halides (or alkenes/alcohols with acid) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to give alkylbenzenes by electrophilic aromatic substitution.
mechanism: AlCl3 helps form R+ (or R–Cl···AlCl3 complex); the benzene π electrons attack R+ forming a sigma complex (arenium ion); loss of H+ restores aromaticity and regenerates AlCl3.
keyPoints: Carbocation rearrangement: n-propyl chloride gives isopropylbenzene as major product
Polyalkylation is common because alkyl is activating - use excess benzene
Fails with strongly deactivated rings (NO2, SO3H, COR, CN) and with –NH2/–NHR (complex with AlCl3)
Not possible with aryl or vinyl halides
Reversible: can transalkylate
whenUsed: Industrial manufacture of ethylbenzene (styrene), cumene (phenol + acetone).
applications: n-Propyl chloride giving cumene by rearrangement
jeeTips: To make n-propylbenzene use acylation then Clemmensen/Wolff–Kishner reduction. Nitrobenzene and aniline do not undergo F–C. Rearrangement: 1° R+ shifts to 2°/3°.

name: Friedel–Crafts Acylation
summary: Benzene is acylated by acid chlorides or anhydrides with anhydrous AlCl3 to give aryl ketones through an acylium ion electrophile.
mechanism: RCOCl + AlCl3 gives the acylium ion RC≡O+, which attacks benzene; loss of H+ gives the ketone (complexed to AlCl3, liberated on aqueous work-up).
keyPoints: No rearrangement (acylium ion is resonance stabilised)
No polyacylation (C=O deactivates ring)
At least one equivalent of AlCl3 needed (ketone product complexes it)
Fails with deactivated rings and amines/phenol –OH complexation
Reduction (Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner) of ketone gives n-alkylbenzene
Benzoyl chloride + benzene gives benzophenone
whenUsed: Preparation of aromatic ketones and straight-chain alkylbenzenes (two-step).
jeeTips: Preferred over alkylation for straight-chain alkylbenzene: acylation then Zn(Hg)/HCl. HCOCl is unstable - use Gattermann–Koch (CO + HCl) for benzaldehyde.

name: Nitration of Benzene
summary: Benzene is nitrated by a mixture of conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 at 50–60 °C through attack of the nitronium ion (NO2+).
mechanism: HNO3 + 2 H2SO4 gives NO2+ + H3O+ + 2 HSO4-; benzene attacks NO2+ to form the arenium ion; loss of H+ gives nitrobenzene.
keyPoints: Electrophile is NO2+ (nitronium ion)
Further nitration (100 °C, fuming HNO3) gives m-dinitrobenzene
–NO2 is deactivating and meta directing
Nitrobenzene is the starting material for aniline (Sn/HCl)
Phenol nitrates readily with dilute HNO3 (o- and p-)
whenUsed: Synthesis of nitroarenes, dyes, explosives (TNT, picric acid) and aniline.

examples.eq: C6H6 + HNO3 ->[\text{conc. H2SO4}][323 K] C6H5NO2 + H2O
C6H5NO2 + HNO3 ->[\text{fuming HNO3, conc. H2SO4}][373 K] m-C6H4(NO2)2 + H2O
C6H5CH3 + HNO3 ->[\text{conc. H2SO4}] o- + p-CH3C6H4NO2 + H2O

jeeTips: Role of H2SO4: acid generating NO2+, not just dehydrating agent. Nitration of aniline in strongly acidic conditions gives significant meta product (anilinium ion).

name: Sulphonation of Benzene
summary: Benzene reacts with fuming sulphuric acid (oleum) or hot conc. H2SO4 to give benzenesulphonic acid by electrophilic attack of SO3.
mechanism: SO3 (or HSO3+) is the electrophile; it attacks benzene to give an arenium ion, which loses H+. The final step gives the sulphonate, which is protonated to –SO3H.
keyPoints: Electrophile: SO3 (neutral but strongly electrophilic S)
Reversible reaction (desulphonation in hot dilute acid/steam)
–SO3H is meta directing and deactivating
Used as blocking group to protect the para position
Toluene sulphonation at higher temp gives p-isomer (thermodynamic)
whenUsed: Making detergents (alkylbenzenesulphonates), phenol (fusion with NaOH), and blocking groups.
jeeTips: Sulphonation is reversible - classic for blocking/ipso questions. SO3H group is a good leaving group under steam.

name: Halogenation of Benzene (FeBr3)
summary: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution with Br2 or Cl2 in the presence of a Lewis acid such as FeBr3, FeCl3 or AlCl3 to give halobenzenes.
mechanism: Lewis acid polarises Br–Br to give Br+ (as FeBr4- Br+); benzene attacks the electrophile forming a sigma complex which loses H+ to FeBr4-, regenerating FeBr3 and giving HBr.
keyPoints: Lewis acid is needed since benzene does not react with Br2 alone (no addition)
Halogens are deactivating but o,p-directing (-I > +M)
Fe + Br2 gives FeBr3 in situ
I2 requires an oxidising agent (HNO3 or HIO3); F2 is too violent
With UV light and excess Cl2, addition gives BHC/gammexane (C6H6Cl6) instead
whenUsed: Preparation of aryl halides for Grignard, Ullmann, Fittig reactions.

examples.note: Addition (BHC) under UV light, not substitution

jeeTips: FeBr3/dark = substitution; UV/excess Cl2 = addition (BHC); Cl2 hv on toluene = side chain. These three conditions are classic traps.

name: Birch Reduction of Benzene
catalyst: Na (dissolving metal), alcohol as proton source
summary: Benzene is partially reduced by Na (or Li) in liquid NH3 with an alcohol as proton source to 1,4-cyclohexadiene, leaving two isolated C=C bonds.
mechanism: Na transfers an electron to the ring giving a radical anion; ROH protonates it to a cyclohexadienyl radical; a second electron gives the carbanion that is protonated to give the 1,4-diene (non-conjugated).
keyPoints: Anti-addition pattern gives non-conjugated 1,4-diene (not 1,3)
Electron-donating groups (OMe, alkyl) end up on the sp2 carbons of the product (2,5 positions)
Electron-withdrawing groups (COOH) end up on sp3 carbon
Alcohol (EtOH) needed as proton source
Anisole gives 1-methoxycyclohexa-1,4-diene
whenUsed: Convert aromatic rings to dienes, e.g. in steroid synthesis.
jeeTips: Not the same as H2/Ni (complete reduction to cyclohexane). Rule: EDG on C=C, EWG on sp3 C in product.

name: Side-Chain Oxidation with KMnO4
summary: Any alkyl side chain with at least one benzylic H is oxidised by hot KMnO4 (or K2Cr2O7/H+) all the way to –COOH, irrespective of chain length.
mechanism: Benzylic C–H is abstracted (benzylic radical/cation stabilised by the ring) and oxidation proceeds via alcohol and carbonyl stages to the carboxylic acid; the rest of the side chain is cleaved.
keyPoints: Needs at least one benzylic H: tert-butylbenzene does not oxidise
Ethylbenzene, propylbenzene etc. all give benzoic acid
Controlled oxidation: CrO2Cl2 (Etard) or CrO3/(CH3CO)2O gives benzaldehyde; MnO2 gives benzaldehyde
Alkaline KMnO4 gives potassium benzoate; acidify to get acid
Ring is not attacked
whenUsed: Preparation of benzoic acids from alkylbenzenes (e.g. terephthalic acid from p-xylene).
jeeTips: Trap: tert-butylbenzene (no benzylic H) is inert. Two different side chains: both oxidised to –COOH (e.g. p-xylene to terephthalic acid). Etard/CrO3-Ac2O stop at aldehyde.

name: Side-Chain Chlorination of Toluene (Cl2/hv)
summary: Toluene undergoes free-radical substitution at the methyl group (not the ring) with Cl2 in sunlight or at boiling point to give benzyl chloride, then benzal chloride and benzotrichloride.
mechanism: Cl2 splits under hv; Cl. abstracts a benzylic H to give the resonance-stabilised benzyl radical, which abstracts Cl from Cl2 to continue the chain.
keyPoints: Light/heat, no catalyst gives side-chain substitution
FeCl3/dark (cold) gives ring substitution (o- and p-chlorotoluene)
Stepwise: C6H5CH2Cl, C6H5CHCl2, C6H5CCl3
Hydrolysis of C6H5CHCl2 gives benzaldehyde; C6H5CCl3 gives benzoic acid
Benzylic radical is stabilised by resonance
whenUsed: Industrial synthesis of benzaldehyde and benzoic acid from toluene.
jeeTips: Memorise: hv/heat = side chain; Lewis acid/dark = ring. Same pairing for bromination (NBS = benzylic).

name: Wurtz–Fittig Reaction
aliases: Alkylbenzene from aryl halide and alkyl halide
summary: An aryl halide and an alkyl halide couple in the presence of sodium in dry ether to give an alkylbenzene.
mechanism: Sodium reacts with both halides to give ArNa and RNa type species (radical or organosodium); the more nucleophilic aryl species attacks the alkyl halide in an SN2-like step forming Ar–R.
keyPoints: Mixed coupling gives also biphenyl (Ar–Ar) and alkane (R–R) as by-products
Aryl halide + alkyl halide gives Ar–R
Extension of Wurtz reaction
Fittig reaction (two aryl halides) gives biaryl
Dry ether essential
Avoid tertiary alkyl halides (elimination)
whenUsed: Preparation of alkylbenzenes such as ethylbenzene and toluene.

examples.eq: C6H5Br + CH3Br + 2 Na ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5CH3 + 2 NaBr
C6H5Br + C2H5Br + 2 Na ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5C2H5 + 2 NaBr
C6H5Cl + CH3Cl + 2 Na ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5CH3 + 2 NaCl

jeeTips: Ar–X + R–X = Wurtz–Fittig; Ar–X + Ar–X = Fittig; Ar–X + Cu = Ullmann. Do not mix these up.

name: Fittig Reaction
aliases: Synthesis of biphenyl from aryl halide
summary: Two molecules of an aryl halide couple with sodium in dry ether to give a biaryl such as biphenyl.
mechanism: Na gives aryl radical / aryl-sodium species which attacks a second aryl halide forming the Ar–Ar bond with loss of NaX.
keyPoints: Aryl halide with Na in ether gives biaryl
Differs from Wurtz–Fittig which uses ArX + RX
Substituted aryl halides give substituted biaryls
Ullmann reaction uses Cu and heat instead of Na
Used for symmetrical biaryls only (mixed halides give mixtures)
whenUsed: Laboratory synthesis of biaryls and polyphenyl compounds.
jeeTips: Product has no alkyl chain (unlike Wurtz–Fittig). Answer for "chlorobenzene + sodium in dry ether" is biphenyl.

name: Ullmann Reaction
summary: Aryl halides (best iodides) heated with copper powder give biaryls through coupling of two aryl groups.
mechanism: Cu inserts into the C–X bond to give an aryl copper(I) species, which reacts with a second ArX through oxidative addition and reductive elimination forming Ar–Ar.
keyPoints: Aryl iodide or bromide coupled with Cu powder at high temperature
Electron-withdrawing o-substituent (e.g. NO2) speeds the reaction
Used for symmetrical biaryls (unsymmetrical gives mixtures)
Alternative to Fittig (Na, ether)
Cu is converted to CuX2 / Cu halide
whenUsed: Synthesis of biphenyls, including hindered or nitro-substituted ones.
jeeTips: Cu powder = Ullmann; Na/ether = Fittig; Na + RX = Wurtz–Fittig. The reaction is distinct from the Gattermann (Cu powder + HX on diazonium salts).

name: Hydrogenation of Benzene to Cyclohexane
conditions: 473 K (or Pt, room temp, high pressure)
summary: Benzene adds three moles of hydrogen over a Ni catalyst at about 200 °C (or Pt/Pd under pressure) giving cyclohexane; no partial reduction stops at cyclohexene.
mechanism: H2 is activated on the metal surface; the adsorbed aromatic ring is hydrogenated stepwise with syn addition, but intermediate cyclohexadiene and cyclohexene are more reactive and hydrogenate immediately.
keyPoints: Heat of hydrogenation of benzene (−208 kJ/mol) is less than 3 × cyclohexene (−360) - resonance energy about 152 kJ/mol
Needs vigorous conditions vs alkenes (room temp)
Cannot be stopped at cyclohexene
Substituted benzenes give cyclohexane derivatives
Compare with Birch (partial, 1,4-diene)
whenUsed: Industrial manufacture of cyclohexane (for adipic acid/nylon).
jeeTips: Resonance energy from heats of hydrogenation is a standard numerical: 3 x 120 - 208 = 152 kJ/mol.

name: Ozonolysis of Benzene
summary: Benzene reacts with three moles of ozone to give a triozonide, which on hydrolytic work-up (Zn/H2O) gives three molecules of glyoxal, supporting the Kekulé structure.
mechanism: Each of the three C=C of the Kekulé structure adds ozone to form an ozonide; reductive cleavage of all three ozonide rings gives 3 OHC–CHO.
keyPoints: Gives only glyoxal: 3 mol from benzene; o-xylene gives glyoxal + methylglyoxal + diacetyl in 1:2:3 ratio
Supports equal C–C bond lengths via mesomerism (Kekulé structures)
Ratio from o-xylene proves oscillation/resonance of double bonds
Benzene needs more drastic conditions than alkenes (resonance stability)
whenUsed: Structural proof for benzene (Kekulé structure); problems on o-xylene ozonolysis ratio.
jeeTips: o-Xylene ozonolysis products in 1:2:3 ratio (glyoxal : methylglyoxal : biacetyl) is a standard Advanced question to justify two Kekulé structures.

name: Desulphonation (Ipso Substitution)
summary: Aromatic sulphonic acids are desulphonated by heating with dilute acid or superheated steam, replacing –SO3H by H (ipso substitution) - the reverse of sulphonation.
mechanism: H+ attacks the ipso carbon bearing SO3H to give an arenium ion, which expels SO3 (as H2SO4 with water) to restore aromaticity.
keyPoints: Reversible electrophilic substitution (ipso attack by H+)
–SO3H used as a blocking group: sulphonate para, substitute ortho, then desulphonate
Thermodynamic vs kinetic: sulphonation favours stable product at high T
Conc. acid favours sulphonation; dilute hot acid favours desulphonation
whenUsed: Removing a blocking group to make ortho-substituted arenes selectively.
jeeTips: Blocking group strategy: SO3H at para -> new group goes ortho -> remove SO3H with steam. Know the ipso concept.
